newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe's Mugabe faces unprecedented criticism.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe's Mugabe faces unprecedented criticism.

text.p: Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, under fire for his handling of labour unrest and frequent trips abroad, is facing the strongest public criticism he has encountered during 16 years in power.
Mugabe, 72, swears to ride out the social and political storm battering his government, and accuses his opponents of using a month-long strike by doctors and nurses to undermine his authority.
Public anger is high in a country grappling with 50 percent unemployment, rising urban poverty and where economic growth has averaged less than one percent annually over the past five years.
Political analyst Chenjerai Hove, one of Zimbabwe's leading writers, accuses Mugabe of driving the southern African state along a familiar African path of social decay.

"Any country that does not care for the health of its citizens becomes a death centre," he said at the weekend, joining several Zimbabweans who rounded on Mugabe's government, in the harshest criticism it has faced since assuming power in 1980.

"The deaths in our hospitals can be laid directly at the door of politicians who are simply unable to exercise flexibility and good sense when called upon to do so," Zimbabwe Independent, a major weekly newspaper, charged.
"The government through its intractable stance has painted itself into a corner. It cannot retract from its current position without losing face," it said.

Mugabe, who attended a world food summit in Rome and left the health strike to his ministers, blames the nurses and doctors for the crisis and refuses to negotiate over their demands for more pay and better conditions.
Last Thursday, three cabinet ministers accused the press of exaggerating the crisis and vowed the government would not give in to the strikers whom it said it had sacked and plans to replace.

Many ministers have been ducking questions on the strike, with Health Minister Timothy Stamps at one stage referring reporters who were badgering him to read the Bible, Amos 5:13. This reads: "In these evil times, the smart thing to do is to keep quiet".
Mugabe and his ZANU-PF party brush aside charges that they have become arrogant and dictatorial over the years in the face of a weak and fragmented opposition.

Analysts say Mugabe seems to prefer to travel the world rather than tackle pressing domestic issues. In the past 10 months Mugabe has been abroad more than 20 times with his new 31-year-old wife, former presidential secretary Grace Marufu.
In August, Mugabe flew for a week-long honeymoon in Cape Town, leaving a majority of Zimbabwe's 180,000 civil servants on the streets demanding higher wages and better working conditions.
He later bowed to pressure and awarded 20 percent pay rises.
His trip to Italy for the food summit drew sharp, unprecedented public criticism.

"Mugabe and (Zairean President) Mobutu (Sese Seko) are the only presidents enjoying themselves in Europe while their countries are burning," wrote political scientist John Makumbe in the weekly Mail and Guardian Newspaper.

"Not only was the visit badly timed but it showed growing and unacceptable arrogance that has become the hallmark of this government's virtual one-party dictatorship of the past decade," commented the independent Financial Gazette newspaper.

The Gazette said the strike by 10,000 of 14,000 state nurses and 500 of 800 doctors reflected social frustrations by a public that believes the political leadership is only interested in feathering its nest, a charge the government vehemently denies.
